name: pipe-and-filter
intent: Decompose a stream- or document-transforming task into a sequence of small independent processing steps (filters) connected by channels (pipes), so each step can be developed, reused, reordered, run in parallel and scaled on its own.
problem: A transformation that is really a chain of steps is written as one monolithic procedure: similar steps are duplicated wherever a comparable job appears, steps cannot be reused across jobs, reordering or inserting a step means editing the whole module, and no single step can be scaled, retried or replaced without touching the others.
context: Record- or byte-stream processing whose overall task decomposes into steps that each consume a well-defined input schema and produce a well-defined output schema, where the chain must be configurable, reusable or able to run at different rates on different machines. It applies from in-process lazy sequences up to a distributed message flow whose pipes are queues or brokers; it needs a stable record contract at every stage boundary and one owner for wiring, start-up and shutdown.
benefits: Composition and reuse: filters with the same external interface can be recombined into new pipelines - add, omit or rearrange stages - without modifying the filters themselves.
Single responsibility per stage makes each transformation small enough to reason about and to test in isolation against its input and output schema.
Independent evolution: a new or replaced filter is a local change; neighbours are unaffected because they depend only on the record contract, not on the stage implementation.
Independent scaling and placement: a slow or resource-hungry stage can be replicated or moved onto suitable hardware while the cheap stages stay where they are.
Streaming execution: records flow through as they become available, intermediates need not be materialised, so latency and memory stay bounded for large data sets.
Concurrency falls out of the structure: stages overlap naturally (pipeline parallelism) and fan-out within a stage adds throughput without changing the filters.
tradeoffs: Plumbing costs: every stage boundary adds buffering, data transfer and often serialisation or copying, so a long chain of trivial steps can be slower and more memory-hungry than one fused loop.
End-to-end throughput is bounded by the slowest filter (and by the pipe buffer size in front of it); the pattern exposes the bottleneck but does not remove it.
Error semantics become explicit work: a failing filter either aborts the chain or needs a declared skip/dead-letter/compensation policy, and a mid-chain failure leaves the stream partially processed.
Distribution converts delivery into an at-least-once problem: retries and redeliveries duplicate records unless filters are idempotent, and parallel stages lose global ordering guarantees.

No shared context: each filter sees only what travels in the record, so correlation data, deadlines and identity must be carried with the payload; stateful, mutually dependent steps cannot be split this way.
Debugging and testing span boundaries: no single stack trace covers the flow, and a change to the pipeline shape requires re-testing the chain end to end rather than one stage.

participants.responsibility: Supplies the initial stream of records (file, socket, query, message channel) and owns the resource being read; it is the first stage and has no inbound pipe.

Performs exactly one processing step: consumes records from its inbound pipe, transforms, filters, splits or enriches them, and publishes the result to its outbound pipe; it knows only its own input and output schema, not its neighbours, and is ideally stateless per record.

Connects one filter's output to the next filter's input, moving records and buffering the difference in rate; it applies backpressure or a bounded-queue policy and contains no transformation or routing logic.
Consumes the terminal stream - collecting into a result, writing to storage, forwarding to another system - and signals completion or failure back to the assembly.

Owns the topology: instantiates and wires filters to pipes, starts and drains the flow, decides the error and shutdown policy; a composition root in-process, a broker/queue topology when the stages are distributed.

use_cases: ETL and document pipelines: parse, validate, normalise, enrich, redact and finally load records into a store.
Request-processing chains in web frameworks where independently testable middleware filters run in a declared order before and after the handler.
Media and image processing chains (decode, resize, watermark, strip metadata, publish) whose steps are reused across different products.
Compiler and analyser front ends: lex, parse, resolve names, type-check and generate code from a stream of tokens.
Log and event ingestion: normalise, redact sensitive fields, enrich with reference data, filter and fan out to several sinks.
Unix-style process pipelines where existing single-purpose executables are composed with real pipes instead of being rewritten as one program.
Apache Beam dataflow: a source PCollection passes through composable PTransforms such as ParDo, Filter and Flatten before a sink, with a runner executing the assembled graph.
Kafka Streams Processor API: source nodes feed processor nodes that transform or forward records to sink nodes; the topology makes stage wiring explicit while allowing processor-local state stores.
POSIX shell pipelines: commands connected with | send each command's standard output to the next command's standard input, composing single-purpose programs through OS pipes.
avoid_when: The transformation is one or two steps: an ordinary function or a simple loop is clearer and faster than a pipeline with its wiring and stage contracts.

The steps are not independent - they share mutable state, must see each other's intermediate results, or have to commit in one transaction: keep them together, or use a coordination pattern such as a process manager instead.
It is a synchronous request-response call with a tight latency budget and no independent scaling need: queue and stage overhead dominate and a plain call chain is enough.
Processing needs evolving, accumulated context rather than a stream of self-contained records (interactive sessions, dialogue, multi-step negotiation): a state machine or process manager fits better.
Reordering and reuse are not requirements and one team owns the whole job end to end: a monolithic procedure or one map/reduce job is simpler to operate.
The payload is large and copying or serialising it at every stage boundary is unaffordable: use zero-copy/chunked streaming or a deliberately fused single pass instead of a naive chain.
anti_patterns: "God filter": one stage that performs several transformations, so the chain can no longer be composed, reordered or tested per step, and the pipeline shape becomes a fiction.
Filters that keep mutable state or reach into globals, silently coupling stages that must be independently replaceable and parallelisable.
Pipes that route, transform or validate records: business logic inside the connector destroys the ability to swap the transport and turns the pipe into a second, undeclared filter.
Unbounded in-memory queues used as pipes, presented as decoupling, until a slow consumer converts the backlog into an outage.

Distributing stages across processes or brokers before the pipeline shape and record contract are stable, multiplying deployment, monitoring and delivery-semantics cost for a flow that changes weekly.
Re-implementing filter/pipe machinery on top of a framework that already provides it (streaming libraries, dataflow blocks, stream processors) instead of using its stages and backpressure.
design_principles: Single responsibility: one well-defined transformation per filter, one transport responsibility per pipe.
Separation of concerns: processing (filter), movement/buffering (pipe), consumption (sink) and wiring (assembly) are separate roles.
Open/closed principle: new behaviour arrives as a new filter that is plugged into the chain, without editing existing filters.
Information hiding and interface segregation: a filter depends only on the record contract at its ports, never on its neighbours' implementations.
Loose coupling as an enabler: because stages communicate only through the record stream, they can be reordered, retried, replicated and distributed independently.
Composition over inheritance: pipelines are assembled from stages rather than expressed by subclassing a monolithic processor.
best_practices: Fix the record contract (schema and version) at each stage boundary before writing filters, and let a filter pass through fields it does not understand unchanged.
Keep filters stateless per record and make any unavoidable side effect idempotent, so retries, redeliveries and parallel instances stay harmless.
Declare the error policy per filter explicitly - fail fast with a dead-letter or error channel, skip and count, or compensate - instead of letting exceptions escape the stage contract.
Bound every pipe (queue capacity, channel buffer, highWaterMark) and decide the overflow behaviour: block/backpressure, drop, or spill, never grow without limit.
Instrument each stage with record counts, latency and error metrics so the bottleneck filter is identifiable from production data.
Wire the whole chain in one composition root; keep filters free of construction, configuration lookup and transport details so they stay testable in isolation.
Start in-process with lazy sequences or streams, and distribute a stage only when it independently needs scale, isolation or a different runtime than its neighbours.
Test filters in isolation against their schema contract and add one end-to-end test over the assembled chain, since pipeline-wide changes cannot be validated stage by stage.
sources: Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad & Stal, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns (1996) - Pipes and Filters (Architectural Patterns, ch. 2).
Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Pipes and Filters (Messaging Systems, ch. 3).
